message.content:
Add a `roundingMode` option to prettyBytes with values 'round' (default, current behaviour), 'floor' and 'ceil', applied to the displayed fraction digits (e.g. 1999 bytes with maximumFractionDigits:1 -> '2 kB' round, '1.9 kB' floor, '2 kB' ceil). It must work together with minimumFractionDigits/maximumFractionDigits, `locale`, `signed` and negative numbers (floor of a negative displayed value should move away from zero in magnitude terms consistently - decide and document). Update index.d.ts and readme.md. The repo uses ava which is not installed and must not be installed; write your tests in test-rounding.js with node's built-in runner (node:test + node:assert) and run `node --test test-rounding.js`.

This is a non-interactive run: nobody will answer questions [clause shortened in the committed copy]. If the spec conflicts with the existing code, decide, document the decision in readme.md, and complete the implementation.

content.content:
1	# pretty-bytes
2	
3	> Convert bytes to a human readable string: `1337` → `1.34 kB`
4	
5	Useful for displaying file sizes for humans.
6	
7	*Note that it uses base-10 (e.g. kilobyte).
8	[Read about the difference between kilobyte and kibibyte.](https://web.archive.org/web/20150324153922/https://pacoup.com/2009/05/26/kb-kb-kib-whats-up-with-that/)*
9	
10	## Install
11	
12	```sh
13	npm install pretty-bytes
14	```
15	
16	## Usage
17	
18	```js
19	import prettyBytes from 'pretty-bytes';
20	
21	prettyBytes(1337);
22	//=> '1.34 kB'
23	
24	prettyBytes(100);
25	//=> '100 B'
26	
27	// Display with units of bits
28	prettyBytes(1337, {bits: true});
29	//=> '1.34 kbit'
30	
31	// Display file size differences
32	prettyBytes(42, {signed: true});
33	//=> '+42 B'
34	
35	// Localized output using German locale
36	prettyBytes(1337, {locale: 'de'});
37	//=> '1,34 kB'
38	
39	// Fixed width for alignment (useful for progress bars and tables)
40	prettyBytes(1337, {fixedWidth: 8});
41	//=> ' 1.34 kB'
42	```
43	
44	## API
45	
46	### prettyBytes(number, options?)
47	
48	#### number
49	
50	Type: `number | bigint`
51	
52	The number to format.
53	
54	A `bigint` of any size is accepted. Past roughly `1e332` bytes the scaled value no longer fits a `number`, and it is written out in full from the exact quotient, so it carries no grouping and no localized decimal separator, the same as a value below `1e-100`.
55	
56	Byte counts are otherwise formatted with the precision of a JavaScript number, which holds about 16 significant digits, so above roughly `1e17` bytes the trailing digits of the output may not be exact. A value that rounds up onto a unit boundary can therefore be printed in the larger unit, so `999499999999999999` bytes is `1 EB` rather than `999 PB`.
57	
58	> [!NOTE]
59	> Rounding uses `Number#toPrecision`, so at an exact tie the direction comes from how that value is stored as a floating point number. `1005` bytes is `1.005 kB` and rounds down to `1 kB`, while `1125` bytes is `1.125 kB` and rounds up to `1.13 kB`.
60	
61	#### options
62	
63	Type: `object`
64	
65	##### signed
66	
67	Type: `boolean`\
68	Default: `false`
69	
70	Include plus sign for positive numbers. If the difference is exactly zero a space character will be prepended instead for better alignment.
71	
72	##### bits
73	
74	Type: `boolean`\
75	Default: `false`
76	
77	Format the number as [bits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bit) instead of [bytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byte). This can be useful when, for example, referring to [bit rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bit_rate).
78	
79	```js
80	import prettyBytes from 'pretty-bytes';
81	
82	prettyBytes(1337, {bits: true});
83	//=> '1.34 kbit'
84	```
85	
86	##### binary
87	
88	Type: `boolean`\
89	Default: `false`
90	
91	Format the number using the [Binary Prefix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_prefix) instead of the [SI Prefix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_prefix). This can be useful for presenting memory amounts. However, this should not be used for presenting file sizes.
92	
93	```js
94	import prettyBytes from 'pretty-bytes';
95	
96	prettyBytes(1000, {binary: true});
97	//=> '1000 B'
98	
99	prettyBytes(1024, {binary: true});
100	//=> '1 KiB'
101	```
102	
103	##### locale
104	
105	Type: `boolean | string | string[]`\
106	Default: `false`
107	
108	- If `false`: Output won't be localized.
109	- If `true`: Localize the output using the system/browser locale.
110	- If `string`: Expects a [BCP 47 language tag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IETF_language_tag) (For example: `en`, `de`, …)
111	- If `string[]`: Expects a list of [BCP 47 language tags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IETF_language_tag) (For example: `en`, `de`, …)
112	
113	> [!IMPORTANT]
114	> Only the number and decimal separator are localized. The unit title is not and will not be localized.
115	
116	> [!NOTE]
117	> A value below `1e-100` bytes needs more than the 100 fraction digits `Intl.NumberFormat` accepts, so it is written out with plain digits instead of a localized decimal separator.
118	
119	```js
120	import prettyBytes from 'pretty-bytes';
121	
122	prettyBytes(1337, {locale: 'de'});
123	//=> '1,34 kB'
124	```
125	
126	##### minimumFractionDigits
127	
128	Type: `number`\
129	Default: `undefined`
130	
131	The minimum number of fraction digits to display.
132	
133	If neither `minimumFractionDigits` nor `maximumFractionDigits` is set, the default behavior is to round to 3 significant digits.
134	
135	Must be an integer between 0 and 100. Throws a `TypeError` for invalid values.
136	
137	Must not be greater than `maximumFractionDigits`, which throws a `RangeError` when both are set.
138	
139	> [!NOTE]
140	> When `minimumFractionDigits` or `maximumFractionDigits` is specified, values are truncated instead of rounded to provide more intuitive results for file sizes.
141	
142	```js
143	import prettyBytes from 'pretty-bytes';
144	
145	// Show the number with at least 3 fractional digits
146	prettyBytes(1900, {minimumFractionDigits: 3});
147	//=> '1.900 kB'
148	
149	prettyBytes(1900);
150	//=> '1.9 kB'
151	```
152	
153	##### maximumFractionDigits
154	
155	Type: `number`\
156	Default: `undefined`
157	
158	The maximum number of fraction digits to display.
159	
160	If neither `minimumFractionDigits` nor `maximumFractionDigits` is set, the default behavior is to round to 3 significant digits.
161	
162	Must be an integer between 0 and 100. Throws a `TypeError` for invalid values.
163	
164	Must not be less than `minimumFractionDigits`, which throws a `RangeError` when both are set.
165	
166	> [!NOTE]
167	> When `minimumFractionDigits` or `maximumFractionDigits` is specified, values are truncated instead of rounded to provide more intuitive results for file sizes.
168	
169	```js
170	import prettyBytes from 'pretty-bytes';
171	
172	// Show the number with at most 1 fractional digit
173	prettyBytes(1920, {maximumFractionDigits: 1});
174	//=> '1.9 kB'
175	
176	prettyBytes(1920);
177	//=> '1.92 kB'
178	```
179	
180	##### space
181	
182	Type: `boolean`\
183	Default: `true`
184	
185	Put a space between the number and unit.
186	
187	```js
188	import prettyBytes from 'pretty-bytes';
189	
190	prettyBytes(1920, {space: false});
191	//=> '1.92kB'
192	
193	prettyBytes(1920);
194	//=> '1.92 kB'
195	```
196	
197	##### nonBreakingSpace
198	
199	Type: `boolean`\
200	Default: `false`
201	
202	Use a non-breaking space instead of a regular space to prevent the unit from wrapping to a new line.
203	
204	Has no effect when `space` is `false`.
205	
206	```js
207	import prettyBytes from 'pretty-bytes';
208	
209	prettyBytes(1337, {nonBreakingSpace: true});
210	//=> '1.34\u00A0kB'
211	
212	prettyBytes(1337, {space: false, nonBreakingSpace: true});
213	//=> '1.34kB'
214	```
215	
216	##### fixedWidth
217	
218	Type: `number`\
219	Default: `undefined`
220	
221	Pad the output to a fixed width by right-aligning it.
222	
223	Useful for creating aligned columns in tables or progress bars.
224	
225	If the output is longer than the specified width, no padding is applied.
226	
227	Must be a non-negative integer. Throws a `TypeError` for invalid values.
228	
229	```js
230	import prettyBytes from 'pretty-bytes';
231	
232	prettyBytes(1337, {fixedWidth: 10});
233	//=> '   1.34 kB'
234	
235	prettyBytes(100_000, {fixedWidth: 10});
236	//=> '    100 kB'
237	
238	// Useful for progress bars and tables
239	[1000, 10_000, 100_000].map(bytes => prettyBytes(bytes, {fixedWidth: 8}));
240	//=> ['    1 kB', '   10 kB', '  100 kB']
241	```
242	
243	## FAQ
244	
245	### Why kB and not KB?
246	
247	`k` is the [standardized SI prefix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_prefix) for kilo.
248	
249	## Related
250	
251	- [pretty-bytes-cli](https://github.com/sindresorhus/pretty-bytes-cli) - CLI for this module
252	- [pretty-ms](https://github.com/sindresorhus/pretty-ms) - Convert milliseconds to a human readable string
253

+> When `minimumFractionDigits` or `maximumFractionDigits` is specified, values are truncated instead of rounded to provide more intuitive results for file sizes, unless [`roundingMode`](#roundingmode) is set.
+How the last displayed digit is rounded.
+- `'round'`: Round to the nearest digit, with ties going away from zero.

+It applies to the fraction digits allowed by `minimumFractionDigits` and `maximumFractionDigits`, or, when neither is set, to the 3 significant digits shown by default. It works with `locale`, `signed`, `binary`, `bits` and `bigint` input.

+**Negative numbers.** `floor` and `ceil` follow the mathematical definition (the same as `Math.floor`/`Math.ceil` and `Intl.NumberFormat`), not the magnitude: `floor` always moves toward negative infinity, so it moves a negative value *away* from zero, and `ceil` moves it toward zero. For any value, `floor` of `-x` prints as `-` followed by `ceil` of `x`. `'round'` is symmetric: ties go away from zero for either sign. The sign comes from the input, so a negative value that rounds to zero still prints as `-0`, the same as without this option.

+**Unit carry.** A value that rounds up onto the next unit is printed in that unit, the same as the default rounding already does, so `999960` bytes with `maximumFractionDigits: 1` and `roundingMode: 'round'` is `1 MB` rather than `1000 kB`. The largest unit (`YB`/`YiB`) never carries.

+> **Why the default is not literally `'round'`.** Before this option existed, the output already used two different behaviors: the 3 significant digit default *rounds*, but `minimumFractionDigits`/`maximumFractionDigits` *truncate* (see the note above). Making `'round'` the default would change existing output, such as `1999` bytes with `maximumFractionDigits: 1` going from `'1.9 kB'` to `'2 kB'`. So when `roundingMode` is omitted the output stays exactly as before. Without fraction digit options that is identical to `'round'`. With them it truncates, so pass `roundingMode: 'round'` to round instead.

+> With the 3 significant digit default, `'round'` keeps using `Number#toPrecision`, so exact ties behave as described under [`number`](#number) (`1005` bytes is `1 kB`). With fraction digit options, rounding goes through `Intl.NumberFormat`, which rounds the shortest decimal form of the value, so `1005` bytes with `maximumFractionDigits: 2` and `roundingMode: 'round'` is `1.01 kB`. For a `bigint` past the `number` range, rounding is exact.

I added the `roundingMode` option (`'round'`, `'floor'`, `'ceil'`). The new tests pass: `node --test test-rounding.js` gives 11/11. I also ran the existing ava suite (`test.js`) with a small stand-in for ava kept outside the repo, so nothing was installed: 48 pass, 0 fail, and 3 skipped, which the repo already marks as skipped.

**Where the spec conflicted with the code: the default isn't literally `'round'`.** The spec called `'round'` both the default and the current behaviour, but those aren't the same today. With `minimumFractionDigits`/`maximumFractionDigits` set, the code currently truncates, so 1999 bytes with `maximumFractionDigits: 1` gives `'1.9 kB'`, not the spec's `'2 kB'`. Making `'round'` the default would have changed existing output and broken existing tests (e.g. `59_952_784 → '59.9 MB'`). So:
- **Option left out:** output is exactly what it was before. Without fraction-digit options it rounds, same as `'round'`. With them it still truncates.
- **Explicit `roundingMode`:** applies to the fraction digits, or to the 3 significant digits when no fraction-digit option is set. Your examples all come out as specified: `'2 kB'` round, `'1.9 kB'` floor, `'2 kB'` ceil.

This decision is written up in readme.md.

**Negative numbers:** `floor` and `ceil` work like `Math.floor`/`Math.ceil`. `floor` always moves toward negative infinity, so it pushes a negative value further from zero: -1999 bytes gives `'-2 kB'` with floor and `'-1.9 kB'` with ceil. `floor` of `-x` always prints as `-` followed by `ceil` of `x`, and the tests check this. `'round'` sends ties away from zero for either sign. The sign comes from the input, so a negative value that rounds to zero still prints `-0 B`, as it already did. `signed` and `locale` work as before.

**Other behaviour worth knowing:**
- **Moving up a unit:** a value that rounds up onto the next unit is shown in that unit, so 999960 bytes with `maximumFractionDigits: 1` and `'round'` gives `'1 MB'`, not `'1000 kB'`. The default rounding already did this; truncation never needs it.
- **Ties at the halfway point:** with no fraction-digit options, `'round'` behaves exactly like the default, so 1005 bytes is still `1 kB`. With fraction-digit options, rounding treats the value as its plain decimal, so 1005 bytes with `maximumFractionDigits: 2` gives `1.01 kB`. This difference is documented.
- **Very large bigints** (past what a regular number can hold) are rounded exactly using bigint arithmetic. Before, that path always truncated.
- **Invalid values** throw a `TypeError`.

**Files:** the logic is in `index.js`. `index.d.ts` gets the type with docs and examples, `readme.md` gets the option section and the decision write-up, and `index.test-d.ts` gets type checks. `tsd` and `xo` weren't run because they aren't installed. The new doc examples do pass the existing test that checks every documented example.
